## How the PSI rules checker works

The PSI rules checker takes one individual’s personal services income for one income year and works through Part 2-42 in the order the Act sets. Each step on the result names the section it applies and what it found.

Income that is not mainly a reward for the individual’s personal efforts or skills is not PSI (subsection 84-5(1)), and income received as an employee falls outside Division 85 (subsection 85-35(1)). A personal services business determination in force settles the question (subsection 87-15(1)). Otherwise the results test comes first: if at least 75% of the PSI is paid for a result, with the plant and tools supplied and liability for defects, the PSI rules do not apply, however much comes from one payer (section 87-18).

If 80% or more of the PSI comes from one payer and its associates, the other 3 tests cannot be self-assessed and only a determination keeps the rules away (subsection 87-15(3)). The checker still works them out, because the Commissioner weighs them for a determination: 2 or more unrelated payers that engaged the individual or entity through offers to the public (section 87-20), principal work by others of at least 20% by market value or an apprentice for half the year (section 87-25), and qualifying business premises all year (section 87-30).

The checker reproduces the conclusion of each worked example in TR 2022/3 that reaches one on a test it applies, and of the matching examples on the ATO’s PSI pages.

## How to enter payers in the PSI rules checker

Enter each payer once, with its associates’ payments added in: the payer is whoever must pay under the contract, so a labour hire firm or agency is the payer, not its client (TR 2022/3 paragraphs 69 to 72). Payers that are associates of each other share one row too, as section 87-20 counts only payers that are not associates of each other. Count each Australian government agency as its own payer (section 87-35) and leave out income received as an employee. If the individual works through their own company, partnership or trust, choose that entity as who receives the income, even if it pays them a salary. Tick ‘Paid for a result’, ‘Supplies plant and tools’ and ‘Liable for defects’ only where the contract or industry custom makes it so (subsection 87-18(4)). The results test counts income, not payers, and a tick covers all of that payer’s PSI: where only part of it meets all 3, leave the boxes unticked, which can only make the results test harder to pass, and work out that part yourself. For the market value of principal work by others, count work by any individual or entity engaged, an individual associate included, but not by an associate that is a company, partnership or trust, nor, for an entity, by an individual whose PSI it receives; a partner counts only if they earn no PSI through the partnership (subsections 87-25(1), (2) and (2A); TR 2022/3 paragraphs 110 to 116). With more than 5 payers, put the smallest together in one row only where every answer is the same; that can only make a test harder to pass.

## What the PSI rules checker leaves to you

The checker does not decide whether income is mainly a reward for personal efforts or skills, whether a contract pays for a result, whether an offer to the public won the work, who is an associate or what principal work is worth. These turn on facts and judgement, so it takes your answers and says so on each step; TR 2022/3 sets out the factors at paragraphs 34 to 49 and 77 to 148.

The checker does not allocate expenses across PSI, business income and other income. Division 85 limits deductions to the extent they relate to PSI (subsection 85-10(1)) but sets no method for the split, and TR 2022/3 leaves deductions to other rulings (paragraphs 6 and 31), so any split is practice rather than law. It does not work out the amount attributed under Division 86, PAYG withholding or a deduction for a net PSI loss.

The checker does not apply the agent rules when they could apply (section 87-40), decide a determination, which is the Commissioner’s (sections 87-60 and 87-65), or test Part IVA, which can still apply to a personal services business (TR 2022/3 paragraph 160). Several individuals working through one entity are tested one at a time (paragraph 76). Confirm the result with the ruling or a registered tax agent.

## How the staff cost calculator works

The staff cost calculator adds up the annual cost of one staff member from figures you supply. Annual cost = wages + supplied super amount + other annual costs. Monthly average = annual cost / 12. Include expected insurance, payroll tax, recruitment, relief staff and equipment in other costs. Paid leave already within salary must not be added again.

No statutory rate or threshold is applied.

## What the staff cost calculator does not decide

The staff cost calculator does not work out super, payroll tax or award pay. The super amount is the figure you enter; the super guarantee rate is a separate table and is not applied by this calculator.

## How the 13-week cash forecast works

The 13-week cash forecast works out closing cash for each week and the funding gap against a buffer you set. Weekly closing cash = opening cash + receipts − payments. Each closing balance opens the next week. Funding gap = minimum buffer − lowest opening or weekly closing cash, with a floor of zero.

No statutory rate or threshold is applied. The layout follows business.gov.au: cash flow.

## What the 13-week cash forecast does not decide

The funding gap is a planning gap, not a lending decision. The 13-week cash forecast does not predict receipts or payments, and weekly totals can hide a shortage within the week. A receipt delayed beyond week 13 is reported separately and does not enter the closing balance.

The Lumbridge cash flow case works the same question with a 45-day receipt delay.

# ATO objection deadline checker: 2 years, 4 years or 60 days

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/business-calculators/objection-deadline/

> The last day to lodge an objection under section 14ZW of the Taxation Administration Act 1953, counted as the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 counts time.

# Objection deadline checker

The last day to object to an income tax or FBT assessment, an amended assessment or another ATO decision, with the weekend rule.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 15 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Objection deadline inputs

Decision objected to Income tax assessment Amended income tax assessment FBT assessment Amended FBT assessment Another decision for which section 14ZW sets no other period Income tax only: does item 1, 2, 3 or 3A of the table in subsection 170(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 apply to the assessment? Yes: 2 years No: 4 years Day notice of the decision was given or served Amended assessments only: day notice of the first assessment for the year was given or served

Item 1 covers most individuals, and items 2 and 3 companies and trusts that are small or medium business entities; each excludes, for example, a scheme to obtain a tax benefit. Item 3A covers their requests to amend. Which item applies is not decided here.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: income tax assessment, item 1, 2, 3 or 3A applies (2 years), notice given 18 November 2026. Period ends, subparagraph 14ZW(1)(aa)(i) Saturday 18 November 2028 Last day to lodge, under subsection 36(2) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 Monday 20 November 2028 If that day is a public holiday where the objection is lodged, or the office is closed all day, it may be lodged on the next day that is not a Saturday, Sunday or holiday. After the last day, an objection needs a written request under subsection 14ZW(2), which the Commissioner decides under section 14ZX.

## How the objection deadline checker works

The objection deadline checker gives the last day to lodge a taxation objection under section 14ZW of the Taxation Administration Act 1953. An income tax assessment allows 2 years after notice of the assessment is given when item 1, 2, 3 or 3A of the table in subsection 170(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1936 applies, and 4 years otherwise. An FBT assessment allows 4 years. Any other decision for which the section sets no other period allows 60 days after notice is served.

An amended assessment allows whichever ends later: 60 days after notice of the amended assessment, or the 2 or 4 years after notice of the first assessment for that year. The checker shows both dates and the later one.

Each period starts the day after notice, because subsection 36(1) of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 leaves out the day a period begins after. A 2-year period from notice given on 28 February 2026 therefore starts on 1 March 2026 and ends on 29 February 2028. When the last day is a Saturday or Sunday, subsection 36(2) lets the objection be lodged on the next day that is not a weekend or holiday. The Act’s own example: a person who has until Saturday 31 March may apply on Monday 2 April.

## What the objection deadline checker does not cover

The checker does not decide whether a decision can be objected to, which item of subsection 170(1) applies, or when notice was given, so keep the notice’s issue and receipt dates. It does not know public holidays: they differ by state and town, so check the last day and the day after it where you lodge. It does not cover private rulings, administrative penalties, retained refunds, deceased estates, specialised taxes or the other decisions for which section 14ZW sets its own period, or the time to seek review of an objection decision. Confirm the date with the notice of decision or a registered tax agent.

# PAYG instalments calculator

One quarter’s PAYG instalment by the instalment amount or the instalment rate, as notified or varied, with any credit to claim.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 15 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

PAYG instalment inputs for one quarter

How this instalment is worked out Option 1: pay the instalment amount at T7 Option 1, varied: an amount from your estimated tax for the year Option 2: instalment income times the rate at T2 Option 2, varied: a rate from your estimates for the year Option 1: instalment amount at T7 (AUD) Option 2: instalment income for the quarter at T1 (AUD) Option 2: instalment rate at T2 (%) Varied amount only: which of this income year’s instalments is this? First: 25% of estimated tax Second: 50% Third: 75% Fourth: 100% Varying only: estimated tax on instalment income for the year, T8 (AUD) Varied rate only: estimated instalment income for the year (AUD) Varying only: earlier instalments this income year, as at 5A (AUD) Varying only: credits claimed at 5B this income year (AUD) Varied rate only: instalment income of the earlier quarters (AUD)

Each option reads only its own fields. Instalment income is generally gross business and investment income, excluding GST.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: instalment rate (option 2), instalment income $20,100.00 at T1, instalment rate 1.7% at T2. T1 × T2 $341.70 Instalment at T11 and 5A, whole dollars $341.00

## How the PAYG instalments calculator works

The PAYG instalments calculator works out one quarterly pay as you go instalment by the method on the activity statement. Under option 1 the instalment is the amount the ATO notifies at T7. Varying it, the first instalment of the income year is 25% of the estimated tax for the year, the second 50%, the third 75% and the fourth 100%, each less the earlier instalments and plus any credits claimed for them. A negative result is a credit to claim at 5B.

Under option 2 the instalment is the quarter’s instalment income at T1 times the instalment rate at T2. A varied rate is the estimated tax for the year divided by the estimated instalment income, times 100. If the varied rate is lower than the earlier rate, the earlier instalments less any credits claimed, less the earlier instalment income times the varied rate, is a credit for 5B.

For 2026-27, the instalment amount the ATO notifies already includes its GDP adjustment of 5%, which raises the base year’s income to allow for growth; the adjustment does not change an instalment rate. The ATO’s own example: instalment income of $20,100 at a rate of 1.7% gives $341.70, entered as 341 at T11 and 5A.

## What the PAYG instalments calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out instalment income, the tax on it or whether you can choose between the 2 options. It does not cover monthly instalments, the 2 instalments a year some payers make, annual instalments or consolidated groups, and it does not estimate general interest charge on a variation that proves too low. It does not check whether you may claim a credit or when an instalment is due. Confirm the figures with the ATO’s PAYG instalments calculator or a registered tax agent.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: genuine redundancy or early retirement scheme payment $48,000.00 after 5 completed years of service, other code R taxable component $0.00, code O taxable component $17,678.00, other taxable payments in 2026-27 $140,000.00, born 1 Aug 1996. Tax-free limit $47,603.00 Tax-free part of the redundancy payment $47,603.00 Code R taxable component $397.00 Withhold from the code R part $127.00 Whole-of-income cap left $40,000.00 Cap for the code O part $40,000.00 Withhold from the code O part $5,657.00 Total to withhold $5,784.00 Under preservation age on 30 June 2027: 32% within each cap and 47% above it.

This is the payer’s withholding under Schedule 11, a payroll and practitioner task; it does not estimate the employee’s take-home pay or the tax assessed on their return.

## How the redundancy and ETP withholding calculator works

The redundancy and ETP withholding calculator works out how much a payer withholds from one life benefit employment termination payment (ETP) made in 2026-27. A genuine redundancy or early retirement scheme payment is tax-free up to $13,598 plus $6,801 for each completed year of service. The part above that limit is a code R ETP, as are payments for invalidity and compensation for personal injury, unfair dismissal, harassment or discrimination. The code R part is withheld at the rate within the cap up to the $270,000 ETP cap and at 47% above it.

The rest of the ETP is code O: a golden handshake, gratuity, non-genuine redundancy payment, severance pay, payment in lieu of notice, unused sick leave or unused rostered days off. Its cap is the smaller of the ETP cap left after the code R part and the whole-of-income cap, which is $180,000 less the other taxable payments you made to the employee in the year. The rate within the cap is 17% if the employee is their preservation age or older on 30 June 2027, otherwise 32%; 47% applies above the cap.

Schedule 11’s example 4 takes Alec, 30, made redundant after 5 years of service with a $48,000 genuine redundancy payment and a $17,678 gratuity, having been paid $140,000 of salary and wages in the year. It works out a $397 ETP over the $47,603 tax-free limit, withholds $127 from it and $5,657 from the gratuity within the $40,000 whole-of-income cap. This calculator opens on those figures, with a date of birth that makes Alec 30, and gives the same amounts.

## What the redundancy and ETP withholding calculator does not cover

The calculator does not decide whether a termination is a genuine redundancy, whether a payment is an ETP or which code applies. It takes the taxable component as you enter it and does not work out a tax-free component other than the redundancy limit, such as an invalidity segment. It covers one life benefit ETP for one termination: not death benefit ETPs, delayed termination payments, a later instalment for the same termination, an earlier ETP in the same year, an employee who has not given you their TFN, a foreign resident or a working holiday maker. It does not work out withholding on unused leave, which Schedule 7 covers. Confirm the figures with Schedule 11 or a registered tax agent.

# Land tax calculator

Land tax for a year in each Australian state and territory that levies it, at the general or trust rates with any foreign owner surcharge, from each revenue office’s current rates.

Published 16 November 2026. Last checked 16 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Land tax inputs

State or territory New South Wales Victoria Queensland Western Australia South Australia Tasmania Australian Capital Territory

Total taxable land value (whole dollars) Rates General rates Trust rates (in Queensland, companies and trustees) Foreign person or absentee owner? No Yes Surcharge value, New South Wales and Tasmania only (whole dollars) All the land is in the Perth metropolitan region (Western Australia)

Enter the value the revenue office taxes, after exempt land is left out: in New South Wales the 3-year average of the land values, in Victoria and South Australia the total site value, in the Australian Capital Territory one parcel’s average unimproved value, and elsewhere the total land value of all the owner’s taxable land. The Northern Territory has no land tax.

Trust rates are a special trust’s in New South Wales, the trust surcharge rates in Victoria, those for companies and trustees in Queensland and those for land held on trust in South Australia. The calculator has none for Western Australia, Tasmania or the Australian Capital Territory.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, total taxable land value $1,100,000.00. Land tax for the year $500.00 Rate applied $100 plus 1.6% of the value over $1,075,000

## How the land tax calculator works

The calculator applies one state or territory’s general or trust scale to a total taxable land value and gives the tax for a full year. Below a jurisdiction’s threshold the tax is nil; the Australian Capital Territory has no threshold, and nor does a special trust in New South Wales. Above it, each scale charges a base amount plus a percentage of the value over a band’s threshold, except that Victoria charges a flat $500 from $50,000 and $975 from $100,000 up to $300,000. South Australia charges for every $100, or part of $100, so the excess is rounded up to the next $100, and RevenueSA issues no assessment where the calculated land tax is under $20; the calculator shows the amount and says so. The Australian Capital Territory adds its fixed charge of $1,778 to the valuation charge and assesses each quarter’s share by its days; the calculator gives the full-year amount. Each scale is the one in force for the land tax year current on 16 November 2026: the 2026 calendar year in New South Wales and Victoria, and the 2026-27 financial year in Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory.

Where a revenue office publishes worked figures, the calculator gives the same amount. Revenue NSW gives $500 on an average land value of $1,100,000, $9,600 for a special trust on $600,000, and $2,100 of land tax and $60,000 of surcharge land tax for a foreign owner of $1,200,000 of residential land. Victoria’s State Revenue Office gives $5,550 on $1,100,000, and its table with the absentee owner surcharge gives $44,650 on $1,000,000 at the general rates. The Queensland Revenue Office gives $1,300 on $680,000 and $87,000 on $6,400,000 for an individual, $106,500 on $6,400,000 for a company, $8,420 on $760,000 for the trustee of a self-managed super fund, and $3,800 on $400,000 for an absentee and for a foreign company, each with $1,500 of surcharge. RevenueSA’s 2026-27 guide gives $2,670 on $1,470,000. Tasmania’s foreign investor land tax surcharge guideline gives $8,000 of surcharge on $400,000. The tests work the rest by hand from the published rates: $6,250 on $1,500,000 in Western Australia with $1,680 of metropolitan region improvement tax, $2,500 at South Australia’s trust rates on $500,000, $3,237.50 on $600,000 in Tasmania and $7,418 on an average unimproved value of $600,000 in the Australian Capital Territory, with $4,500 of foreign ownership surcharge.

## Trust rates, surcharges and the metropolitan region improvement tax

Trust rates are a special trust’s rates in New South Wales, with no threshold; the trust surcharge rates in Victoria; the rates for companies and trustees, including super funds, in Queensland; and the trust rates in South Australia. Western Australia taxes a trustee’s land as if it were the trustee’s own, at the general rates.

A foreign or absentee owner pays: in New South Wales surcharge land tax of 5% of the land value of the residential land a foreign person owns, their share only and including land exempt from land tax, entered as the surcharge value; in Victoria the absentee owner surcharge of 4% of the total taxable value, from $50,000 at the general rates and from $25,000 at the trust rates; in Queensland the absentee rates for an absentee individual, and for an absentee, a foreign company or the trustee of a foreign trust a surcharge of 3% of the value over $350,000; in Tasmania the foreign investor land tax surcharge of 2% of the assessed land value of the foreign-owned share of residential General Land acquired on or after 1 July 2022, entered as the surcharge value; and in the Australian Capital Territory the foreign ownership surcharge of 0.75% of the parcel’s average unimproved value.

Western Australia charges its metropolitan region improvement tax of 0.14% of the value over $300,000 with land tax where the land is in the Perth metropolitan region; the calculator adds it when all the land is. A surcharge and this tax are shown apart from the land tax, with the total.

## What the land tax calculator does not compute

The land tax calculator applies the scale for the rates and owner you choose. It does not decide which land is taxable, which rates apply, whether an owner is a foreign person or absentee, or what the taxable or surcharge value is; the foreign purchaser surcharge calculator applies each jurisdiction’s test of a foreign or absentee owner. These are not computed:

- New South Wales: exemptions and concessions, including the principal place of residence and primary production land exemptions, exemptions from surcharge land tax, and land of a company that is not its group’s concessional company, which pays 1.6% of its whole taxable value with no threshold, or 2% of it where the group’s land exceeds the premium threshold (Land Tax Act 1956, Schedule 13, Parts 3 and 4).
- Victoria: exemptions and concessions, exemptions from the absentee owner surcharge and vacant residential land tax.
- Queensland: exemptions and relief, exemptions from the foreign surcharge and the aggregation of land held for trusts with the same beneficiaries.
- Western Australia: land tax exemptions, and the metropolitan region improvement tax on holdings only partly in the Perth metropolitan region.
- South Australia: exemptions, waiver or relief, and which land held on trust qualifies for the general rates.
- Tasmania: zero rate classifications, exemptions and rebates, including principal residence and primary production land, and which land the foreign investor land tax surcharge applies to.
- Australian Capital Territory: land tax exemptions, when the foreign ownership surcharge applies, a unit’s share by its unit entitlement and the split into quarters. Land tax there applies to residential property that is not a principal place of residence.

Joint ownership, grouping of related companies and the apportionment of the tax between properties are not computed either. Confirm the figure with the revenue office’s own calculator or assessment notice before relying on it.

# Transfer duty calculator

General transfer (stamp) duty on a residential purchase in any Australian state or territory, from each revenue office’s current rates, and the duty for an eligible first home buyer.

Published 15 November 2026. Last checked 16 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Buyer General rates Eligible first home buyer, established home Eligible first home buyer, new home

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, dutiable value $1,350,000.00. General transfer duty $55,537.00 Rate applied $52,237 plus $5.50 for every $100, or part of $100, over $1,290,000

## How the transfer duty calculator works

The transfer duty calculator applies one state or territory’s general rates to a dutiable value. Most scales charge a base amount plus a rate for every $100, or part of $100, over a threshold, so the excess is rounded up to the next $100. Victoria takes a percentage of the excess without rounding it, and 5.5% of the whole value from $960,000 to $2 million. The Australian Capital Territory takes $4.54 per $100 of the whole value above $1,455,000. The Northern Territory uses a formula up to $525,000 and a single percentage of the whole value above it.

Where a revenue office publishes worked figures, the calculator gives the same amount. Revenue NSW’s worked examples give $55,537 on $1,350,000, $14,437 on $450,000 and $203,237 on $4,000,000; its Transfer of Land or Business Calculator gave $14,441.50 on $450,050 when tried on 15 November 2026. The Victorian State Revenue Office gives $28,070 at the standard rate on $550,000 and $19,070 on $400,000. The Queensland Revenue Office gives $31,275 on $850,000. RevenueSA’s foreign ownership surcharge example gives stamp duty of $26,830 on $600,000. The Tasmanian duty calculator gave $18,247.50 on $500,000 on 15 November 2026. For Western Australia, the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory the tests work examples by hand from the published rates: $32,315.50 on $800,000 in Western Australia, $17,880 on $650,000 in the Australian Capital Territory and $23,928.60 on $500,000 in the Northern Territory.

## Duty for a first home buyer

For an eligible first home buyer, the calculator applies the state or territory’s first home buyer concession on a home, new or established, bought to live in. Each scheme’s conditions, such as citizenship or residency, never having owned a home, age and moving in within a set time, are in the sources listed and are not tested.

- New South Wales: no duty up to $800,000. Below $1 million, the duty on $800,000, scaled down evenly to nil at $1 million, comes off the general duty, with the $20 minimum.
- Victoria: no duty up to $600,000. Up to $750,000, the general duty multiplied by the value over $600,000 and divided by $150,000.
- Queensland: the home concession rate less the first home concession amount for the value’s $10,000 band, from $17,350 below $710,000 down to nil from $800,000, so no duty up to $700,000. No duty on a new home, whatever its value.
- Western Australia: no duty up to $600,000. Up to $800,000, $16.15 for every $100, or part of $100, over $600,000.
- South Australia: no duty on a new home, whatever its value. An established home pays the general rate.
- Australian Capital Territory: no duty under the Home Buyer Concession Scheme, whatever the value. The scheme is open to buyers who have not owned property in the past 5 years, not only first home buyers.
- Tasmania and the Northern Territory: no first home buyer duty concession on a home, so the general rate applies. Tasmania’s exemption for established homes ended with settlements on 30 June 2026.

The NSW Government’s 2026-27 table gives $9,796.75 on $850,000, $19,593.50 on $900,000, $29,390.25 on $950,000 and $37,227.65 on $990,000. Revenue NSW’s First Home Buyers Assistance calculator gave $38,991.06 on $999,000 and $20 on $800,001 when tried on 16 November 2026. The Queensland Revenue Office gives $6,555 on $730,000 and $24,100 on $850,000 for an established first home. For Victoria and Western Australia the tests work examples by hand: $24,713.33 on $700,000 in Victoria and $16,150 on $700,000 in Western Australia.

First home owner grants are payments to the buyer, not duty concessions, and are not computed: New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania, the Northern Territory’s HomeGrown Territory Grant, and the Australian Capital Territory’s First Home Owner Grant, which stopped on 1 July 2019.

## What the transfer duty calculator does not compute

The transfer duty calculator gives general transfer duty, and duty for an eligible first home buyer of a home. It applies no other concession, exemption or surcharge, does not test whether a buyer is eligible, and does not decide whether a transaction is dutiable or what its dutiable value is; the foreign purchaser surcharge calculator works out the foreign purchaser duty surcharge. These are not computed:

- New South Wales: duty on land other than residential land over $3,870,000, which the premium rate does not reach (the calculator applies it and says so in its result), the First Home Buyers Assistance Scheme on vacant land, surcharge purchaser duty for foreign persons, including foreign trusts and companies, and landholder duty.
- Victoria: the principal place of residence concession, the first home buyer concession on vacant land, the off-the-plan concession, the City of Melbourne new residential property concession and exemption, the pensioner exemption and concession, and foreign purchaser additional duty.
- Queensland: the home concession for a buyer who is not a first home buyer, the first home vacant land concession, and additional foreign acquirer duty, which also reaches companies and trusts.
- Western Australia: the concessional rate for a principal place of residence or WA business asset up to $200,000, the first home owner rate on vacant land, the off-the-plan concession or rebate, and foreign transfer duty.
- South Australia: stamp duty relief for eligible first home buyers on vacant land, seniors downsizing stamp duty relief, home buyer ex gratia relief for victim-survivors of family, domestic or sexual violence, and the foreign ownership surcharge.
- Tasmania: concessions and exemptions, and the foreign investor duty surcharge.
- Australian Capital Territory: the lower rate for an eligible owner occupier transaction (Table 1 of the determination), the Home Buyer Concession Scheme on vacant land, and the rates for commercial property.
- Northern Territory: the house and land package exemption and the home incentive schemes in Part 5 of the Act.

Duty on a trust acquisition, a landholder or corporate trustee acquisition, a lease premium or a business sale, and the land tax that follows a purchase, are not computed either. Confirm the figure with the revenue office’s own calculator or a conveyancer before relying on it.

## How the income tax calculator works

The income tax calculator works out one individual’s tax for a full income year from 2020-21 to 2026-27: the tax on taxable income at the year’s rates, the offsets, the Medicare levy and the Medicare levy surcharge. The offsets are the low income tax offset and, for 2020-21 and 2021-22, the low and middle income tax offset. It then takes that total, and any study or training loan repayment, from the tax withheld you enter, to estimate a refund or an amount owing.

An Australian resident pays nothing on the first $18,200 and then each part of taxable income at its rate. The low income tax offset of up to $700 comes off a resident’s tax, but not below nil. The Medicare levy is 2% of a resident’s taxable income; up to the low-income threshold there is none, and from there to the phase-in limit it is 10% of the income over the threshold, if that is less. The ATO’s example on Medicare levy reduction for low-income earners, read 17 November 2026, gives Angie, single with $29,000 of taxable income in 2025-26, a levy of $98.90, as this calculator does.

The Medicare levy surcharge applies to a resident without private patient hospital cover whose income for surcharge purposes is above the year’s threshold. For each day without cover it charges 1%, 1.25% or 1.5% of taxable income and reportable fringe benefits, by the tier the income falls in.

For 2026-27 the Medicare levy thresholds are those the Act held on 17 November 2026, the same as 2025-26. If Parliament raises them for 2026-27, a person just above $28,011 will pay less than shown here.

## What the income tax calculator does not compute

The calculator gives the tax of one person who was a resident, a foreign resident or a working holiday maker for the whole year. It does not compute:

- the Medicare levy reduction for families, which depends on family taxable income and dependants, or a Medicare levy exemption;
- the seniors and pensioners tax offset and its higher Medicare levy thresholds, or any other offset, such as for private health insurance, dependants or super contributions;
- a change of family or cover status during the year beyond the days without cover, the private health insurance rebate, a spouse’s trust income that the surcharge test adds, the net amount on which family trust distribution tax has been paid, which counts in income for surcharge purposes and in the amount the surcharge is levied on, or exempt foreign employment income, which the ATO’s surcharge page adds to income for surcharge purposes when taxable income is $1 or more;
- a first home super saver released amount, which is taxed with a 30% offset but left out of repayment income and income for surcharge purposes, or, for 2023-24 and earlier, the taxed element of a super lump sum up to the low rate cap, which a person from preservation age to under 60 could leave out of income for surcharge purposes;
- a study loan debt smaller than the repayment: the repayment cannot exceed what is still owed (section 154-20(1)(c) of the Higher Education Support Act 2003), which the calculator does not ask for;
- a part-year resident’s reduced tax-free threshold, a working holiday maker who is an Australian resident, or one with other income besides working holiday taxable income;
- tax on superannuation or employment termination remainders, income averaging, or a minor’s unearned income;
- Division 293 tax, excess contributions, PAYG instalments or other credits besides the tax withheld you enter.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s Simple tax calculator or a registered tax agent.

## How the take-home pay calculator works

The take-home pay calculator takes one salary for a year, month, fortnight or week and works out the year’s income tax, offsets, Medicare levy, any Medicare levy surcharge and any study or training loan repayment on it. Salary sacrificed to super comes off first. From 2026-27 it also takes off the standard deduction of up to $1,000 for work-related expenses. It then gives what is left for the year, a month, a fortnight and a week, and the super guarantee an employer must pay, which goes to a super fund and is not part of take-home pay.

Those take-home amounts are the year’s tax spread evenly: the year’s net amount divided by 12, 26 and 52. They are not the amounts an employer withholds each pay. For a weekly, fortnightly or monthly pay in 2026-27, the calculator also works the PAYG amount withheld from one pay under the ATO’s Schedule 1, and Schedule 8 with a study loan, and the year’s withholding less the year’s tax, which is the refund or amount owing when the tax return is assessed. For earlier years, and for working holiday makers, who are withheld from under another schedule, use the ATO’s tax withheld calculator.

The example on arrival is 2025-26, before the standard deduction: on $75,000 the Medicare levy is $1,500, as the ATO’s example of Matthew on What is the Medicare levy gives. In 2026-27 the same salary is $74,000 of taxable income.

When the salary includes super, the calculator splits it: at 12%, a package of $112,000 is $100,000 of salary and $12,000 of super. Super guarantee stops at the year’s maximum contribution base, so above it the super stays at the most the base allows.

## What the take-home pay calculator does not compute

The calculator assumes one employer, a salary paid evenly over the full year, and no other income, deductions or offsets. It does not compute:

- overtime, bonuses, allowances or leave loading, a 53rd weekly or 27th fortnightly pay, or withholding on scale 1, scale 5 or 6 or for a working holiday maker, a withholding declaration’s offsets or a Medicare levy variation;
- work-related deductions you claim, which reduce the standard deduction dollar for dollar except those section 25-130(3) disregards, such as professional association fees;
- salary sacrifice of anything but super, reportable fringe benefits, excess concessional contributions or Division 293 tax;
- everything the income tax calculator leaves out, such as the Medicare levy reduction for families and the seniors and pensioners tax offset;
- a family’s surcharge: this calculator works out the surcharge for a single person with no dependants, and the income tax calculator works out a family’s;
- a study loan debt smaller than the repayment, which section 154-20(1)(c) of the Higher Education Support Act 2003 caps at what is still owed;
- whether an employee is entitled to super guarantee, the lower transitional rate for employees on Norfolk Island (11% for 2026-27), or a second employer’s separate maximum contribution base;
- super guarantee pay by pay: the calculator works it on the year’s earnings, rounded once, where an employer works it on each payday from 2026-27, so the year’s total can differ by cents, and to 2025-26 on each quarter’s earnings, so above the base a weekly or fortnightly salary with more pays in some quarters gets less: $260,000 paid fortnightly in 2025-26 can give $29,400, not $30,000.

Confirm the figures with the ATO’s Simple tax calculator or a registered tax agent.

## How the lump sum in arrears calculator works

Salary, wages or a Centrelink or compensation payment that you receive as a lump sum, for earlier years, is taxed in the year you receive it, often at a higher rate than it would have been in the years it was for. The tax offset gives back the difference. The calculator first tests whether the arrears are at least 10% of the rest of your normal taxable income for the year. If they are, it works out the tax the arrears add this year and the tax they would have added in the years they accrued in, and the offset is the amount by which the first exceeds the second.

For the 2 latest accrual years it adds the arrears to that year’s taxable income at that year’s resident rates. Arrears from any earlier years are taxed at the average of those 2 years’ rates, so the oldest years’ arrears can share one row. Where a recent year was itself a year you got this offset for, or arrears of such a year accrued in it, its income is adjusted as the Act directs.

The ATO’s page on lump sum payments in arrears works Yan’s breakdown of arrears by year, received in 2025-26. The calculator opens on it; the ATO does not give Yan’s taxable incomes, so the $100,000, $30,000 and $17,000 are fictional. Anthony’s, Sudeep’s and Heather’s examples are among the boundary cases.

## What the lump sum in arrears calculator does not cover

The calculator works the offset for a person resident in Australia for the whole of the year of receipt and of each recent accrual year, entitled to the full tax-free threshold, for a year of receipt of 2024-25, 2025-26 or 2026-27. It does not decide what is a lump sum in arrears: it takes the arrears you enter as eligible income that accrued more than 12 months before you received it. It refuses an employment termination payment, unused leave paid on termination, a super lump sum or income stream, above-average special professional income or primary producer averaging in the year of receipt or a recent accrual year, and does not cover a minor’s income or a trustee.

It does not work out the Medicare levy or surcharge on the arrears, which have their own rules, or apply the offset against your tax. The ATO works the offset when you lodge with the amounts for each year; confirm the figures with the ATO or a registered tax agent.

# Study and training loan calculator

Inputs: 2026-27, taxable income $60,470.00, reportable fringe benefits $5,400.00, total net investment loss $1,330.00, reportable super contributions $16,500.00, exempt foreign employment income $2,680.00. Repayment income $86,380.00 Compulsory repayment $2,527.80 15% of repayment income over $69,528 up to $129,717, and 17% of any part above it.

## How the study and training loan repayment calculator works

The study and training loan repayment calculator works out the compulsory repayment on a HELP, VET Student Loan, Student Start-up Loan or Australian Apprenticeship Support Loan debt for one income year. It first adds up repayment income: taxable income, reportable fringe benefits, total net investment loss, reportable super contributions and exempt foreign employment income.

From 2025-26 the repayment is marginal: nothing up to the minimum repayment income, then 15 cents for each dollar above it up to a second threshold and 17 cents above that, unless 10% of all repayment income is less. For 2026-27 the minimum repayment income is $69,528 and the second threshold $129,717, and 10% is the lesser amount from $186,051. For 2024-25 one percentage of the whole repayment income applied, from 1% above $54,434 to 10% from $159,664.

The boundary cases below take the inputs of the 4 worked examples on the ATO’s thresholds and rates page, read 17 November 2026, and work each one from section 154-20. For Barry’s 2026-27 repayment income of $137,064, section 154-20(2) gives 15% of the $60,189 from $69,528 to $129,717, which is $9,028.35, plus 17% of the $7,347 above $129,717, which is $1,248.99: $10,277.34 in all. For Branson’s 2024-25 repayment income of $99,736, the 5.5% rate gives $5,485.48.

## What the study and training loan repayment calculator does not compute

The calculator gives the compulsory repayment for one income year. It does not compute:

- the cap at the debt you still owe, or voluntary repayments;
- the overseas debtors repayment levy on worldwide income for a foreign resident (section 154-16);
- whether no repayment is due because your Medicare levy is not payable or is reduced under section 8 of the Medicare Levy Act 1986 (section 154-1(2));
- the amounts an employer withholds each pay for a loan, which the take-home pay calculator works for 2026-27, or indexation of the debt;
- years before 2020-21.

Confirm the figure with the ATO’s Study and training loan repayment calculator or a registered tax agent.

# Payroll tax calculator

One employer’s annual payroll tax for 2026-27 in any Australian state or territory, step by step, each step cited to its Act or revenue office.

Published 17 November 2026. Last checked 17 November 2026.

JavaScript is required for interactive calculations. The formula, assumptions and source links remain available below.

Payroll tax inputs for 2026-27

State or territory New South Wales Victoria Victoria, regional employer (at least 85% of taxable wages paid to regional employees) Queensland Western Australia South Australia Tasmania Australian Capital Territory Northern Territory

Taxable wages in the state or territory for 2026-27 (AUD) Total Australian wages for 2026-27, taxable and interstate (AUD; leave blank if all are paid in that state or territory)

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, taxable wages $1,500,000.00, total Australian wages $1,500,000.00. Deduction (Revenue NSW: threshold times NSW wages over Australian wages) $1,200,000.00 Taxable amount: wages less the deduction $300,000.00 Payroll tax at 5.45% on $300,000.00 (Revenue NSW: thresholds and rates) $16,350.00 Payroll tax $16,350.00 An estimate for 2026-27 for one employer that is not a member of a group and pays wages all year, before any exemption, rebate or discount.

## How the payroll tax calculator works

The payroll tax calculator estimates one employer’s payroll tax for the whole of 2026-27 in one state or territory. Each jurisdiction allows a deduction or tax-free threshold, which an employer that also pays wages elsewhere in Australia shares in proportion to its wages there. Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory reduce the deduction as Australian wages grow, until it reaches nil. The result shows the deduction, the amount taxed, the tax at each rate and, in Victoria and Queensland, each surcharge or levy on its own line, with the provision applied.

Where a revenue office publishes worked figures, the tests hold them. Revenue NSW: $1,500,000 of NSW wages are taxed on $300,000, and $900,000 of $3,000,000 has a threshold of $360,000. The Victorian State Revenue Office: $80 million in Victoria and $70 million in New South Wales give surcharge thresholds of $5,333,333.33 and $53,333,333.33. The Queensland Revenue Office: $1,356,789 of $1,789,776 has a deduction of $932,460 to the dollar. RevenueWA: annual wages of $1,104,000 give $6,600; its other 2 examples round the deduction to the dollar and come out 1 and 3 cents lower than this calculator. RevenueSA: $800,000 of $1,600,000 has a deduction of $300,000 and $500,000 of $2,000,000 one of $150,000. The Tasmanian State Revenue Office: $2,400,000 gives $54,400, and $2,400,000 of $3,000,000 gives $72,800. The ACT Revenue Office and the Territory Revenue Office publish no worked figures that could be read, so the tests work examples from the Acts by hand: $84,375 on $3,000,000 in the Australian Capital Territory and $41,250 on $3,000,000 in the Northern Territory. This calculator opens on Revenue NSW’s first example.

## What the payroll tax calculator does not compute

The payroll tax calculator gives one annual estimate and no advice. It does not decide which payments are taxable wages or where they are taxable, and does not cover:

- an employer that is a member of a group, whose threshold and rate depend on the group’s wages and which members share the deduction;
- an employer that paid wages for only part of 2026-27, whose threshold every jurisdiction reduces by the days it employed;
- monthly or other periodic returns, and the annual reconciliation of amounts already paid;
- exemptions, rebates and discounts, such as Queensland’s apprentice and trainee rebate and its 1% discount for regional employers, claimed in the return, and the ACT’s 6.85% cap for an eligible university;
- any year other than 2026-27.

Confirm the figure with the revenue office or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

## How the SGC and Payday Super calculator works

From 1 July 2026, under Payday Super, an employer owes super guarantee for each payday, and the employee’s fund must receive it within 7 business days, or a longer period for a first contribution, out-of-cycle pay or an ATO determination. The calculator finds that due date from the site’s business days calendar, then works out the super guarantee charge for one employee if the fund received less than 12% of qualifying earnings by then: the final shortfall still unpaid at the assessment, notional earnings at the GIC rate on the amount that was late, and the administrative uplift, reduced if the ATO had not itself assessed or estimated the employer’s SG charge from 1 July 2026 to the payday, and for a voluntary disclosure. A contribution counts from the day the fund received it with what it needs to allocate it to the employee. For a quarter that ended by 30 June 2026 it applies the old law instead: the shortfall at that year’s charge percentage, 10% nominal interest and the $20 administration component.

## What the SGC and Payday Super calculator does not cover

The calculator gives an estimate for one employee and one payday or quarter, and no advice. It does not cover:

- the choice loading for not meeting choice of fund obligations;
- the late payment offset under the old section 23A for quarterly contributions made late;
- bunched contributions under section 18C(2) item 4;
- a contribution made from 1 to 28 July 2026 that item 186 of the transition applies first to a shortfall for the quarter ending 30 June 2026: count only what is left of it;
- a disclosed contribution with no receipt day, whose notional earnings section 36(3) works out as if the fund received it 7 business days after it was paid;
- exemption certificates, and amounts paid that have not reached the fund;
- GIC and penalties once the charge is payable;
- paydays after 30 June 2027, whose maximum contributions base is not yet known, and quarters before July 2022.

Confirm the figure with the ATO or a registered tax agent before relying on it.

## How the company tax and franking calculator works

The calculator applies the base rate entity test of section 23AA of the Income Tax Rates Act 1986 to this year’s figures: aggregated turnover under $50 million, and base rate entity passive income of no more than 80% of assessable income. A base rate entity pays 25% of its taxable income, and any other company 30% (subsection 23(2)).

The rate for franking a dividend comes from a second test. Section 995-1 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 runs the base rate entity test on the previous year’s turnover, passive income and assessable income, so a company can pay tax at 30% and frank at 25%, or the reverse; a company that did not exist in the previous year franks at 25%. The maximum franking credit is the dividend times 1 over the gross-up rate, which is 100% less that rate, over that rate (section 202-60): one third of the dividend at 25% and three sevenths at 30%. A credit above the maximum is taken to be the maximum (section 202-65).

The shareholder includes the dividend and its franking credit in assessable income and gets a tax offset equal to the credit (section 207-20). Tax at the marginal rate you enter, less the offset, is the extra tax the dividend brings; where the offset is larger, an individual gets the excess refunded (section 67-25).

The calculator reproduces the outcome of each ATO example: Happy Feet (3.8% passive income, 25%), Coffee and Cake (28.6%, 25%), Best Equity (100%, 30%), SoftDev (85%, 30%) and Hats 4 Cats ($170 million of aggregated turnover, 30%). For Dillmore Manufacture’s $100,000 dividend franked at 30% it gives $42,857.14, the exact credit; the ATO rounds the gross-up rate to 2.3333 and shows $42,857.75, which is more than the section 202-60 maximum.

## What the company tax and franking calculator does not cover

The calculator does not work out aggregated turnover, assessable income or base rate entity passive income: enter figures you have established, with the turnover of connected entities and affiliates included, as the ATO’s Hats 4 Cats example shows. Taxable income gives the tax before offsets, PAYG instalments and other credits.

Not covered: the rates of RSA providers and pooled development funds (subsections 23(3) to (5)), life insurance companies (section 23A), not-for-profit companies and credit unions; corporate unit trusts and public trading trusts; and income years before 2021-22, when the base rate was 27.5% or 26%. A shareholder that is a company, trust, super fund or non-resident is outside its scope; a company shareholder cannot have excess franking credits refunded (section 67-25). Franking account balances, franking deficit tax, the benchmark rule and the holding period rule are not tested: the company tax and franking worksheets track the franking account and the benchmark rule. Have a registered tax agent confirm the figures and the result.

## How the foreign buyer surcharge calculator works

The calculator applies the chosen state or territory’s own test of who is foreign to your answers, once for its duty surcharge and once for its land tax surcharge, as each revenue office states them. The duty surcharge is its rate times the dutiable value of the buyer’s share: 9% in New South Wales, 8% in Victoria, Queensland and Tasmania (1.5% on Tasmanian primary production land), and 7% in Western Australia and South Australia. The ACT and the Northern Territory charge none.

The land tax surcharge is for a full land tax year on the land value you enter: 5% in New South Wales, 4% in Victoria from $50,000 of taxable land ($25,000 for a trust), 3% of the value over $350,000 in Queensland, 2% in Tasmania and 0.75% in the ACT. Western Australia and South Australia charge none, and the Northern Territory has no land tax. Victoria charges a fixed trust’s surcharge on the land held for absentee beneficiaries only. The general transfer duty is worked on the whole property, for all buyers together, at the general rates.

The calculator reproduces the revenue offices’ examples: Revenue NSW’s $90,000 of surcharge purchaser duty and $39,187 of transfer duty on $1 million, and $60,000 of surcharge land tax on $1.2 million; Victoria’s $80,000 for Andrew, $16,000 for Emily’s $200,000 share and $20,000 for Clara’s half of a fixed trust’s $1 million; RevenueSA’s $42,000 and $21,000 for Peter; Western Australia’s $14,000 for Simon; Queensland’s $1,500 on $400,000; and Tasmania’s $8,000 on $400,000.

## Who is foreign in each state and territory

An individual who is an Australian citizen, holds a permanent visa or is a New Zealand citizen on a special category visa is not foreign for Queensland, Western Australian, South Australian and Tasmanian duty. New South Wales also requires a permanent resident or New Zealand citizen to have been in Australia 200 days of the previous 12 months (Revenue Ruling G009); Victoria gives a New Zealand citizen no exception unless they ordinarily reside in Australia for 6 consecutive months around settlement. Victorian and Queensland land tax charge absentees: non-citizens without a permanent visa who do not ordinarily reside in Australia and were away on the day or for over 6 months of the year.

A company is foreign when it is incorporated outside Australia, or foreign persons with associates hold 50% or more (more than 50% in Victoria) of its shares or votes, or in New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and Western Australia of its potential voting power. New South Wales instead asks whether one foreign person with associates holds 20% or more, or foreign persons together 40% or more, wherever the company is incorporated. Trusts and super funds follow the same shares of capital or members’ balances. Victorian land tax counts absentee interests instead, which you enter apart: a company pays absentee owner surcharge when absentees hold more than 50%, a fixed trust on the land held for absentee beneficiaries, and a complying super fund none. A foreign person who ordinarily lives in Australia is no absentee.

A discretionary trust is foreign in New South Wales if a foreign person could benefit, now or by amending the deed (section 104JA); in Victoria and Tasmania if foreign persons could be given more than 50%, or 50% or more, of the capital; in Queensland if foreign takers in default hold 50% or more; in Western Australia if a foreign person controls it, as a foreign trustee or appointor does, or foreign takers in default hold 50% or more; in South Australia if a trustee, appointor, named object or taker in default is foreign; and in the ACT only if a named foreign beneficiary could receive 50% or more. Victorian land tax looks only at named (specified) beneficiaries who are absentees.

## What the foreign buyer surcharge calculator leaves to you

The calculator does not decide exemptions, refunds or ex gratia relief, which each Commissioner grants on application. Among them are Australian-based developers and build to rent in New South Wales and Victoria, exempt permanent residents who live in the home in New South Wales, significant contributors and large developers in Queensland, and refunds when a buyer stops being foreign within 12 months in South Australia. When one is sought, it refuses. It also refuses a partner (provisional) or retirement visa holder, whom the revenue offices treat differently, and does not trace interests through other companies and trusts or decide who is an associate.

Not covered: the Commonwealth’s foreign investment application fees and its restrictions on foreign purchases of established homes from 1 April 2025, which RevenueSA notes; landholder and corporate trustee acquisitions; concessions on general duty; Queensland’s absentee land tax rates, which replace the general rates; Victorian trust surcharge rates; control of a Western Australian discretionary trust by a foreign person other than its trustee or appointor, such as one whose consent a distribution needs; control of a Victorian company through its board or through influence the Commissioner finds, rather than through shares or votes; a Victorian beneficiary nomination for trust land bought before 2006, under which the surcharge starts at $50,000 rather than $25,000; joint land tax assessments; property converted to residential use later; and a surcharge charged again when a buyer becomes foreign within 3 years. The transfer duty calculator and the land tax calculator work the general duty with first home concessions and the general land tax. Confirm the result with the revenue office or a registered adviser before relying on it.

Work out Business days between 2 dates The date a number of business days after the start The date a number of business days before the start Public holidays of Australian Capital Territory New South Wales Northern Territory Queensland South Australia Tasmania Victoria Western Australia Any state or territory: skip a holiday that applies throughout any of them Start date End date, to count between 2 dates Number of business days, to find a date

The count starts the day after the start date and includes the end date. Dates run from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2027, and to 31 August 2027 for Victoria and for any state or territory.

Calculate Fictional example: the first boundary case below. Change the inputs and calculate your own. Inputs: New South Wales, start 21 December 2026, end 4 January 2027. Business days after the start, to and including the end 7 Weekday public holidays skipped 25 December 2026 (Christmas Day), 28 December 2026 (Boxing Day / Boxing Day (observed) / Proclamation Day (observed)), 1 January 2027 (New Year's Day) Part-day and regional holidays count as business days; where a local day replaces Melbourne Cup Day or the WA King’s Birthday, the state date is still skipped.

## How the business days calculator works

The calculator skips Saturdays, Sundays and the public holidays of the state or territory you choose, using each government’s published dates for 2026 and 2027. Between 2 dates, it counts the business days after the start date up to and including the end date, so a Friday to the next Monday is 1. Forward or back, it finds the date that is that many business days after or before the start, and lists each weekday holiday it skipped.

‘Any state or territory’ skips a day that is a public holiday throughout any one of them, as the site’s Payday Super business days table counts them, and leaves out Melbourne Cup Day and the WA King’s Birthday because neither applies throughout its state.

## What the business days calculator does not cover

Part-day holidays, such as the evenings of Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve in South Australia and the Northern Territory, count as business days. So do regional holidays, among them the Royal Queensland Show in Brisbane, Tasmania’s Royal Hobart Regatta and Recreation Day, and show days, and days off for one group only, such as Tasmania’s Easter Tuesday for the public service. A council or region’s local substitute for Melbourne Cup Day or the WA King’s Birthday is not applied: the state date is still skipped.

The calculator does not decide whether a law counts business days, clear days or calendar days, or which state’s holidays apply. Dates after 31 December 2027 are refused until the governments confirm the following year, and Victorian dates after 31 August 2027 until the AFL schedules its Grand Final. The calculator does not work out a superannuation guarantee or Payday Super due date.

# Privacy and site use

# Privacy and site use

The duguid.com.au privacy notice explains how the site handles browser calculations, hosting and feedback.

Published 12 September 2026. Last reviewed 4 November 2026.

## Browser calculations

The website’s calculators process the figures you enter in your browser. They do not send those figures to a server or save them in browser storage. Download any results you want to keep before leaving the page. Downloaded files stay wherever you save them.

The accounting-question search also runs in your browser. It does not send search text to a search service. It does place the search term and topic in the page address so a filtered list can be bookmarked or shared, which means the term appears in your browser history and in any address you pass on.

## Cookies and analytics

The website’s own code does not set cookies or include advertising pixels. Its fonts, images and application scripts are served from this domain.

No analytics script is delivered. Cloudflare Web Analytics is switched off, so I receive no page-view reports. GitHub Pages and Cloudflare still process requests to host and protect the site, as the Hosting section below describes.

Email Address Obfuscation is disabled so email links work without scripts. The address is public in the HTML pages, their plain-text alternates and the machine-readable index. The contact page also spells it out for anyone whose browser does not open an email app.

Cloudflare also asks browsers to report network errors to Cloudflare for seven days and to prefetch pages you are likely to open next (the nel, report-to and speculation-rules response headers). Neither carries the figures you type into the calculators. A prefetched or shared page address can carry question-search terms, because the search places them in the address; do not put confidential information in a search you may share or leave in your history.

On a sample of page loads, Cloudflare adds a report-only security policy header, which asks your browser to tell Cloudflare which scripts the page loads and which connections it makes. It blocks nothing. A report includes the page address, which can hold question-search terms, but not the figures you type into the calculators. If Cloudflare treats a request as suspicious, it can answer with its own verification page, which runs Cloudflare’s code and may set a security cookie; see Cloudflare’s cookie documentation. Cloudflare makes these additions itself; they are not part of this website’s source. The calculators work out their figures in your browser without sending them to a server.

When you select Human or Machine view, your browser saves that display preference on this device. The preference is not sent to a server. You can change it with the view switch or remove it by clearing this site’s browser storage.

## Hosting

GitHub Pages hosts this website’s files, and Cloudflare delivers them to your browser. These providers process technical information about visits, which may include IP addresses, request details and security or performance data. See the GitHub Privacy Statement and Cloudflare Privacy Policy for their handling of that information.

## Feedback and external links

Do not include taxpayer information, client files or other confidential records. An email stays in my mailbox until I delete it, GitHub keeps issues public in its own systems under its terms and I cannot delete copies other people hold.

GitHub issues are public. Links to GitHub and other websites take you to services with their own privacy policies. Software you download or install has its own documented data handling; this notice covers the website.

To ask what personal information I hold, have it corrected or complain about how I handled it, email that address, or take a complaint about the handling of personal information to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner. Other project links are on the Contact page.

# Profit vs cash flow: an Australian Excel worked example

Source: https://duguid.com.au/examples/profit-vs-cash-flow/

> A fictional Newcastle business holds quarterly profit at $35,957.55 AUD while one late $44,000 receipt leaves cash $25,160 short. Workbook, figures and limits.

# Profit vs cash flow: an Australian Excel worked example

How can a business report a profit and still run short of cash? Because profit records the sale and cash records the day the money arrives.

The worked example moves one receipt by 45 days: quarterly profit stays at $35,957.55 and the bank account falls $25,160 below zero.

Download the Excel example Compare the two cases

To run the experiment, open the workbook, change Assumptions!B2 from 0 to 45 and compare quarterly profit with the lowest daily cash balance. Read the full steps.

XLSX, 23,506 bytes. Needs desktop Excel with automatic calculation. The explanation and results below can be read without Excel.

Lumbridge Services is fictional. Every business, customer, invoice, balance and date here is fictional, and all amounts are Australian dollars (AUD). No client outcome is described.

Published 18 September 2026. Last reviewed 28 September 2026.

One receipt arrives 45 days late. Weekly closing cash falls to ($25,160) against a $15,000 buffer. Compare both cases. Exported from Excel on 4 November 2026; capture record.

## The business and the question

Lumbridge Services is a fictional maintenance business in Newcastle, NSW. It bills two service lines, Varrock maintenance and Falador repairs, and invoices $60,000 of work each month: $40,000 Varrock and $20,000 Falador, before GST. The forecast covers the quarter from 1 October to 31 December 2026.

The owner wants to buy equipment. The quarter shows a profit, so the money looks available. The question is whether the bank account can carry the business to the end of December if one customer pays late.

The model holds every other assumption still. Monthly materials are $12,000 and overhead $6,000. Gross wages are $24,000 a month, with $19,000 paid to employees, $5,000 of PAYG withholding and $2,880 of super. The opening bank balance, receivables, payables, GST, loan and tax instalment all come from fictional 30 September 2026 balances. The owner’s policy is to keep $15,000 in the bank.

## The one change: a 45-day delay

Invoice OPEN-V is September work for the Varrock line: $40,000 plus $4,000 GST, so $44,000 is banked. The baseline case receives it on 14 October 2026. The late case receives the same $44,000 on 28 November 2026, 45 calendar days later.

Nothing else changes. The work was performed in September either way, the invoice was issued either way and the customer pays in full either way. Only the day the money lands moves.

The workbook exposes that single control. Assumptions!B2 holds the delay in whole calendar days and accepts 0 to 120. The main comparison uses 0 and 45 days; the sensitivity table also checks 15, 30 and 60 days.

## Both cases, side by side

Same work, same customer, different receipt date. All amounts AUD.

Forecast measure | Receipt on time | Receipt 45 days late
Quarter revenue | $180,000.00 | $180,000.00
Profit before income tax | $35,957.55 | $35,957.55
October customer receipts | $66,000.00 | $22,000.00
October closing cash | $32,040.00 | −$11,960.00
First day the bank account is negative | None in the quarter | 28 October 2026
Lowest daily closing cash | $16,800.00 on 7 October | −$25,160.00 on 6 November
December closing cash | $67,320.00 | $67,320.00

The two cases end the quarter with the same cash because the delayed receipt still arrives, on 28 November. That later recovery cannot pay the wages, supplier invoices and GST that fall due in late October and early November.

Against the owner’s $15,000 buffer, the late case is $40,160 short at its worst day. A reader looking only at December closing cash, or only at profit, sees neither the shortfall nor its date.

Weekly closing cash in the late case, exported from the distributed workbook in Excel 16.0 on 4 November 2026. The 13 plotted values are $16,800, $15,600, $25,520, ($11,960), ($11,960), ($25,160), $17,640, $27,560, $49,680, $36,480, $79,280, $67,320 and $67,320, against the assumed $15,000 buffer. Capture record.

## Compare five receipt delays

A 15-day delay is enough to put this fictional business below zero for one day. Longer delays can also extend the time below zero without changing the lowest balance. These five runs move only the $44,000 OPEN-V receipt from its original 14 October date.

Daily closing cash at five receipt delays. All amounts AUD; all dates are in 2026.

Delay in days | Receipt date | Lowest cash | First date at that low | Days below zero
0 | 14 October | $16,800.00 | 7 October | 0
15 | 29 October | −$11,960.00 | 28 October | 1
30 | 13 November | −$25,160.00 | 6 November | 16
45 | 28 November | −$25,160.00 | 6 November | 16
60 | 13 December | −$25,160.00 | 6 November | 22

Quarterly profit before income tax stays at $35,957.55 and December closing cash at $67,320 in every run. Another scheduled customer receipt on 13 November explains why the 30- and 45-day cases have the same 16 days below zero. The 60-day case includes a further negative period later in November.

Days below zero counts all negative daily closing balances, including separate periods. It does not measure intraday liquidity. The comparison tests five selected delays, not every possible receipt date, and assumes no funding facility.

Calculated on 26 September 2026 with the Python model at the same captured source commit, 386c7ff. All 455 daily balances across the five runs were independently reconciled to the dated source receipts and payments; each monthly cash reconciliation was $0.00. This is a Python calculation record, not a new Excel verification. Read the results, definitions and source hashes (JSON).

## Why profit did not move

Profit is measured on the accrual basis. Lumbridge earned the OPEN-V revenue when it performed the work in September, so the sale sits in the September accounts in both cases. Moving the receipt changes the debtor balance, not the revenue, and no expense changes either. Quarterly profit before income tax is $11,985.85 a month in both cases, or $35,957.55 for the quarter.

Cash is measured on the day money moves. The payments the business owes do not wait for a customer. In the late case, October receipts fall from $66,000 to $22,000, while the same $63,960 of payments still leaves the account. Those payments include materials on 7 October, the September-quarter GST of $12,600 and a $3,000 income tax instalment on 28 October, and net wages and super on 28 October.

The model states the bridge between the two. It starts from profit, adds back depreciation of $200 a month and the non-cash leave provision of $2,254.15 a month, adjusts for the movement in gross receivables and the GST liability, then subtracts the $1,000 monthly loan principal and the tax instalment. A separate direct cash schedule ties to that bridge exactly: the model’s reconciliation difference is $0.00 in every month of both cases.

Three obligations are still outstanding at 31 December in both cases: $12,600 of GST, $5,000 of PAYG withholding and $13,200 of supplier invoices. The $67,320 closing balance is not spendable surplus.

## The decision for a person

The model does not approve or refuse the equipment purchase. It gives a reviewer three things to act on:

- Confirm the OPEN-V receipt date with the customer before committing to discretionary spending.
- Resolve the funding gap between 28 October and mid-November, which the model neither borrows nor overdraws. No overdraft, new loan or owner contribution is assumed anywhere in this forecast.
- Compare actual collections with the forecast each week, because the whole result turns on one date.

Whether the business should defer the purchase, arrange finance or accept the risk is a judgement about a real business with real customers. This example supplies the arithmetic, not that judgement.

Needs desktop Excel with automatic calculation. No Xero login, add-in, macro or AI agent is used, and the workbook contains no macros and no external links.

## Rebuild it from source

The example lives in the au-fpa-pack repository, an Australian extension of Jeff Brines / Guiderail’s openfpa. From a checkout of the captured commit, with Python 3.11 and uv:

```
uv sync --locked --extra dev
uv run --locked --extra dev python examples/lumbridge-services/models/generated/lumbridge.py
uv run --locked --extra dev python examples/lumbridge-services/models/generated/lumbridge.py --delay-days 45
```

Each run writes the workbook, briefing and schedules to examples/lumbridge-services/output/ and verifies all 21 monthly workbook lines against the Python model before replacing the workbook. Expect quarter_profit_before_tax of 35957.55 in both runs, and minimum_daily_cash of 16800.0 on 2026-10-07 at a 0-day delay and -25160.0 on 2026-11-06 at 45. A rebuilt workbook can differ in package metadata or cache bytes from the file distributed here.

Read the source and assumptions at the captured commit.

To reproduce the additional sensitivity rows, run the same command with --delay-days 15, --delay-days 30 and --delay-days 60. Each run replaces the output files, so retain its results before starting the next one. Count values below zero in the resulting daily-cash.csv ending-cash column to reproduce days below zero.

## Limits

The Lumbridge case is a fictional demonstration, not a client result. No forecast accuracy, client outcome or time saving has been measured.

- The only supported scenario is the receipt delay, from 0 to 120 whole calendar days. Revenue, wages and operating assumptions are fixed.
- Payment dates, PAYG withholding, workers compensation, the tax instalment and the loan terms are supplied scenario assumptions, not statutory calculations. PAYG withholding is a flat $5,000 a month, not a withholding table result.
- Payroll tax is nil because annualised wages and super of $322,560 sit below the bundled $1.2 million NSW threshold for a single ungrouped employer. Grouping and interstate wages need separate assessment.
- Daily balances net everything dated on the same day. They do not establish intraday liquidity or the order in which payments clear.
- The output is not a complete forecast statutory balance sheet, and it does not calculate company income tax expense.
- The example does not test when a super fund receives a contribution. Payday Super timing covers that question.

Varrock and Falador are Old School RuneScape naming references. No game assets or prices are used, and no affiliation with Jagex is claimed. No game knowledge is needed.

## Common questions

### How can a business make a profit and still run out of cash?

Profit records revenue when the work is performed and cash records money when it arrives. In this example the September work stays in September profit whether the $44,000 invoice is banked on 14 October or 28 November, so a 45-day delay leaves quarterly profit at $35,957.55 while the bank account falls to minus $25,160 on 6 November.

### What changes between the two cases?

One date. Invoice OPEN-V, worth $40,000 plus $4,000 GST, is received on 14 October 2026 in the baseline and on 28 November 2026 in the late case. Revenue, expenses, wages, supplier terms and every other payment date are identical.

### Why do both cases end December with the same cash?

The delayed receipt still arrives inside the quarter, on 28 November, so both cases close December at $67,320. The recovery is too late to fund the payments due in late October and early November, which is why the daily view matters more than the closing balance.

### Is this a real client case?

No. Lumbridge Services, its customers, invoices and balances are fictional. No client outcome, forecast accuracy or time saving is claimed.

# Ozzit: Excel LAMBDA functions for Australian modelling

Source: https://duguid.com.au/tools/ozzit/

> A free Excel workbook of 150 native LAMBDA functions and 5 help tables for Australian modelling: GST, financial years, AASB 16 leases and amortisation.

# Ozzit

The Ozzit workbook holds 150 functions and 5 help tables for GST, financial years, depreciation, loans and leases, and every definition is visible in Excel.

Current release Ozzit v3.7.0, 18 November 2026, from the Ozzit repository. Published 18 September 2026. Last reviewed 19 November 2026.

Delivery

Excel workbook

Needs

Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later

Boundary

Calculates only. The reviewer decides the accounting treatment and the tax position.

Download Ozzit v3.6.0 Browse worked formulas

XLSX, 485,256 bytes. Needs Microsoft 365 or Excel 2024 or later. No add-in or macro.

## Extract GST from $1,100

```
=oz.GSTExtractλ(1100)
```

100.00 displayed to two decimal places

Assumes a wholly taxable, GST-inclusive amount at 10%. Read the workings, the Excel check and the limits.

## What Ozzit is

An Excel workbook, not a program. Open it, copy a function into your own model, and the formula travels with the file. Every definition is a native LAMBDA stored as a defined name, so the arithmetic stays inside the workbook where a reviewer can read it.

The v3.6.0 workbook carries 155 named formulas: 150 LAMBDA functions and 5 help tables that document them inside the workbook. Each module also ships an editable demonstration worksheet, and the formula source is published as plain text in the repository’s src/ folder and indexed in functions.csv.

The Australian helpers are deliberately small: GST addition and extraction with a 10% default rate, a 1 July financial year label, 5 helpers for the ATO’s small business benchmark ratios, 2 modelling depreciation schedules and 4 AASB 16 lessee schedules. The rest of the library is general financial modelling.

Release v3.6.0 adds 7 functions: oz.Varianceλ and oz.VariancePctλ for budget variance, oz.FinancialMonthλ, oz.FinancialQuarterλ and oz.YearToDateλ for financial-year periods, oz.LevelPaymentλ for a level loan payment when each period has its own rate, and oz.CorkscrewRateλ for a corkscrew whose interest runs on the average of each period’s opening and closing balances. Each has its entry in the index below.

## Who it is for and what it needs

Ozzit suits an accountant or analyst who builds models in Excel and wants the working visible rather than hidden in an add-in or a macro. It is not a bookkeeping tool, and it never touches a ledger.

What the workbook needs. Scroll sideways on small screens.
